strengths: Clear problem formulation with three well-motivated properties (P1-P3) for skill-based continual learning
Sound experimental methodology with proper ID/OOD splits to evaluate compositional transfer and generalization
Fair baseline comparisons using equivalent parameter budgets (LoRA, Prompt Tuning with same soft token length)
Comprehensive ablation studies examining token length, composition complexity, and initialization strategies
Thorough documentation with extensive appendices enabling reproducibility of synthetic experiments
Honest and detailed limitations discussion acknowledging key practical challenges
Well-written and clearly organized paper with effective visualizations
weaknesses: Experiments limited exclusively to synthetic digit-sequence transformations (ASC, ADD, SHIFT, etc.), which is far from realistic language understanding or reasoning tasks
No validation on real NLP tasks; the perfectly compositional nature of digit operations does not reflect realistic skill dependencies
Unvalidated claims about skill-centered dataset construction; suggested approaches (LLM annotation, educational datasets) are not demonstrated on actual realistic tasks
Model scale limited to 500M parameters (Qwen2.5-0.5B); generalization to larger models (7B-70B+) is undemonstrated and computational feasibility for large-scale models is questionable
Incomplete baseline coverage; no comparison to continual learning methods from ML literature (EWC, SI, rehearsal) or recent lifelong learning work in LLMs
Insertion functions are task-specific and ad-hoc (Table 2), suggesting the method requires domain knowledge; generality across different task types is unclear
Limited technical novelty: the approach is primarily a straightforward combination of existing techniques (soft tokens + skill-centric training)
Zero-shot composition property demonstrated only in synthetic setting; unclear whether it holds for real language understanding where skills may be interdependent

strengths: Clear problem formulation with well-defined properties (P1, P2, P3) addressing real limitations of existing continual learning approaches
Insightful Section 4 showing pretrained LLMs naturally contain tokens encoding procedural knowledge (XOR/XNOR experiments on real models)
Rigorous methodology within the controlled setting: explicit skill definitions, clean ID/OOD splits, comprehensive ablations on token length, composition complexity, and initialization
Honest and transparent discussion of limitations (dataset construction, scope, soft token instability, computational cost) in Appendix C
Well-designed synthetic experiments with appropriate baselines (LoRA, Prompt Tuning, ICL) and controlled parameter counts
weaknesses: Severely limited experimental scope: all main experiments restricted to single synthetic task (digit transformations) on one small model (0.5B); zero validation on any natural language tasks despite claiming practical continual learning contribution

Skill-centered dataset construction is fundamentally impractical: proposed methods (explicit mapping, LLM annotation, curated datasets) are inapplicable or unvalidated for real tasks; paper provides no guidance on real-world dataset construction

Core properties underperform: Property 2 shows 16-25% OOD accuracy drops (Figure 4); Property 3 zero-shot composition degrades to near-zero accuracy at difficulty (Figure 5) and underperforms ICL despite 100k training samples vs. ICL's 50-200 examples
Unclear how approach applies to realistic tasks: skills are implicit/entangled in real NLP, insertion function design underspecified, no path for adaptation to domains like QA or summarization

Unfair baseline comparisons: LoRA/Prompt Tuning designed for task-centric adaptation (testing on skill-centric data is somewhat circular); no comparison to other continual learning methods; ICL baseline limited to 100 examples

Incremental technical contribution: straightforward combination of existing techniques (soft tokens from prompt tuning, vocabulary integration from Hewitt et al., skill-centric training); limited methodological novelty; relies on pre-trained compositional abilities from prior work

Unresolved soft token instability: Appendix C acknowledges 'optimization instability' but provides no solutions; Table 6 shows random initialization brittleness (0.63±0.32 vs. 0.85±0.06 for INV-POL, 26% gap); no convergence analysis or mitigation strategies

Scalability and generalization concerns: all experiments on small models (0.5B-8B); no computational cost measurements vs. baselines; unclear scaling to 13B+ models; only 2 new skills learned; no analysis of data quality/diversity effects

Missing practical details: insertion function design is task-specific and underspecified; no guidance on choosing functions for new domains; 'skill' abstraction loosely connected to formal framework; potential for hierarchical/overlapping skills unexplored

Disconnect between motivation and main contribution: Section 4 motivates with real models (XOR/XNOR) but main experiments entirely synthetic; limited transferability of insights from toy domain to real tasks

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation with clear limitations of existing approaches (catastrophic forgetting, in-context learning constraints, task-specificity of prompt tuning)
Principled empirical motivation via Section 4 showing pretrained LLMs naturally develop skill tokens (XOR vs. XNOR), providing evidence for vocabulary-level approach
Controlled experimental design using synthetic digit-sequence tasks enabling explicit sample-skill mappings, unambiguous composition rules, and clean ID/OOD evaluation splits
Comprehensive validation of three target properties: P1 (no weight updates by construction), P2 (consistent OOD compositional transfer), P3 (convincing zero-shot composition vs. ICL)
Thorough ablation studies revealing capacity-regularization trade-offs (token length effects), benefits of composition complexity in training, and initialization robustness
Transparent acknowledgment of limitations (dataset construction challenges, proof-of-concept scope, soft token sensitivities, computational costs) strengthens credibility
Extensive reproducibility support through detailed appendices with hyperparameters, implementation details, and computational specifications
weaknesses: Severely limited experimental scope: only synthetic digit-sequence transformations far removed from realistic NLP; trivial skills (sorting, adding) vs. real compositional semantics; small model (Qwen2.5-0.5B); only 2 new skills demonstrating scalability is unproven

Skill-centered dataset construction remains underspecified: only explicit construction validated, LLM metacognition approach undemonstrated despite being cited as a key practical mechanism; critical bottleneck for real-world applicability
Insertion function φ_S requires manual design per skill with no principled guidance; clear scalability barrier for arbitrary new skills in realistic settings

Shallow theoretical justification: no formal analysis of why vocabulary-level integration outperforms prefix-level for composability; 'limited capacity as inductive bias' is intuitive but not rigorously established

Performance degrades substantially with complexity: accuracy drops from ~60% to ~20% across sequence lengths (Figure 5); OOD gaps of 15-25 percentage points (Figure 4) suggest approach doesn't fully solve compositional transfer even in controlled settings

Limited baseline comparisons: primarily LoRA and Prompt Tuning; ICL only in one section; missing recent continual learning and compositional generalization methods; no comparison to other prefix/adapter approaches
Lack of interpretability analysis: no visualization of soft tokens, no probing experiments to understand captured knowledge (syntactic vs. semantic vs. procedural), limiting mechanistic insight
Computational cost not fully resolved: full model backpropagation required, making it comparable to fine-tuning; impractical for large models (>30B); advantage over fine-tuning unclear
Limited experimental breadth: only 2 new skills, single architecture, small model; scalability to 5-10 skills and larger models (7B+) undemonstrated
Gap between synthetic proof-of-concept and realistic applications is substantial and undemonstrated; generalization claims to natural language tasks remain speculative

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear gap analysis (Table 1) and important application to continual learning
Rigorous experimental methodology on controlled synthetic task with precise in-distribution/out-of-distribution splits enabling clean evaluation of compositional properties
Strong performance on compositional transfer (Figure 4): skill neologisms achieve 84% OOD accuracy vs. LoRA 0.60 and prompt tuning 0.57, supporting core hypothesis
Novel capability of zero-shot composition of independently learned skills, not easily achievable with existing PEFT methods
Comprehensive ablation studies (skill token length, composition complexity, initialization, label noise) providing mechanistic insights
Clear presentation with good visual exposition (Figures 1-2) and explicit algorithms; generous experimental details in appendices
weaknesses: Limited real-world validation: Skill-Mix experiment uses only 300 training samples, 2 skills, and 50 test queries; results show modest improvements (~75% accuracy with both skills composed) with large gap between synthetic and NLP settings
Incremental novelty: core contribution is prompt tuning + skill-centered training combination; skill neologisms closely follow Hewitt et al. (2025) with main innovation being the training regime

Strong assumption that skill-centered datasets can be constructed; practical feasibility varies widely; NLP methods (LLM annotation, expert curation) introduce costs and quality concerns; no systematic evaluation of dataset quality/diversity impact

Incomplete validation of motivating claims: Section 4 (XOR/XNOR) uses only 4 models on 2 operations; claim that 'XOR' token encodes procedural knowledge is suggestive but not definitive; no deeper analysis of what procedural knowledge is captured

Overselling of 'zero-shot composition': reduces to inserting both tokens in context; unclear whether representations are genuinely composable or model handles composition via in-context learning; limited ablation distinguishing true compositional structure

Computational costs underexplored: backpropagation through full model makes training 'comparable to fine-tuning in practice' but no timing comparisons provided; scaling to >30B parameter models noted as challenging
Missing important comparisons: no evaluation against other continual learning or compositional mixture-of-experts approaches; in-context learning baseline somewhat weak

Natural language experiment reliability concerns: GPT-5 grading for reproducibility; only 2 skills tested; no error analysis or qualitative failure examples; representativeness of Skill-Mix evaluation unclear

strengths: Clear problem formulation with three well-defined, testable properties (P1-P3)
Rigorous synthetic experiments with comprehensive ablations examining token length, composition complexity, initialization, and label noise robustness
Honest acknowledgment of significant practical limitations (dataset construction, computational cost, optimization instability)
Clever motivating experiment (Section 4) showing pretrained models encode procedural knowledge in vocabulary tokens
Comprehensive experimental details enabling reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited novelty: primarily combines skill-centered training (a data construction strategy) with vocabulary-level soft tokens (incremental over prompt tuning and Hewitt et al. 2025)
Insufficient mechanistic understanding: paper doesn't explain why independently trained soft tokens compose zero-shot or why vocabulary integration enables this better than prefix-based approaches
Severely limited natural language validation: only 2 skills, 1 model, 50 test samples; results show modest gains (75% skill neologisms vs. 80-90% LoRA/prompt tuning on trained skills)

Significant practical constraints inadequately addressed: skill-centered dataset construction is difficult; 20% label noise degrades performance substantially; computational cost comparable to fine-tuning
Narrow experimental scope: Section 5 uses only 0.5B model on synthetic tasks; no evaluation on larger models (7B+); gap between controlled experiments and realistic settings is substantial
Incomplete baselines: no comparison of skill-centered training on prompt tuning alone; ICL baselines limited to 10-100 examples; missing comparisons to other PEFT and skill composition methods
Sensitivity issues: Table 6 shows large variance with random initialization (INV-POL: 85±6% vs. 63±32%), suggesting inherited optimization instability from prompt tuning
Skill definition mismatch: framework relies on restrictive closed-form assumption; natural language skills are much fuzzier, and the gap isn't addressed

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear articulation of limitations in existing approaches (fine-tuning, in-context learning, prompt tuning)
Thorough experimental validation on synthetic task with proper ID/OOD split design following established skill composition framework (Arora & Goyal)
Novel combination of skill-centered training with vocabulary-level soft token integration; insight that limited capacity provides inductive bias for composability (Section 5.3.1)
Strong zero-shot composition results: independently trained skill neologisms substantially outperform in-context learning (Figure 5)
Comprehensive ablation studies examining token length, composition complexity, initialization, and label noise with clear insights
Validation on natural language task (Skill-Mix) demonstrates broader applicability beyond synthetic domains
Excellent presentation with clear figures and reproducible experimental details; comprehensive appendices with hyperparameters and implementation details
Honest discussion of limitations and open challenges (soft token optimization, dataset construction, computational costs)
weaknesses: Core contribution is somewhat incremental: applies existing soft token/prompt tuning techniques with skill-centered training; limited novelty over prior work on soft prompts and neologisms

Skill-centered dataset construction is significant practical limitation under-addressed in main text; Section 3.3 lists potential sources but provides limited concrete guidance; label noise experiment (Figure A4) shows 20% noise degrades performance with no solutions proposed

Computational cost and soft token optimization challenges downplayed: training requires full backpropagation (comparable to fine-tuning per Appendix C), sensitivity to hyperparameters partially addressed but remains concern

Section 4 motivation is suggestive but incomplete: XOR/XNOR experiment shows frequency correlation but doesn't definitively prove skill tokens emerge from pretraining; lacks deeper analysis of why keywords improve performance

Natural language evaluation (Section 6) is limited in scope: only 2 skills, 50 test samples, high baseline accuracy (~80%) reduces impact of zero-shot composition results; missing comparison to directly relevant work (STAT, He et al. 2026) and Skill-Mix baseline results
Limited analysis of why vocabulary-level integration specifically improves compositionality versus prefix-based approaches; insertion function ϕ shown only via examples without ablation

Scalability claims in title not fully supported: practical constraints (dataset construction, optimization instability, computational costs) suggest limited near-term scalability; theoretical justification for why skill-centered training enables composability lacking
Gap between Section 4 (pretrained skill tokens) and Sections 5-6 (learning new skills) could be stronger; design choices not always justified (e.g., mean of pretrain embeddings for initialization)
